headline: Forget the Fluke Boats — The Rock Pile at Jones Inlet Is Where the Real Work's Getting Done
subhead: While the fleet grinds out short fluke in Sloop Channel, the night bite on bass at the inlet jetty is quietly the best thing going this week.
body_markdown:
Every boat I know is stacked up in Sloop Channel right now working the fluke drift like it's the last week of summer that matters. I get it — it's easy fishing, chartreuse bucktail and a strip of squid, drift the drop-off, wait for the thump. But I've been telling guys at the bait shop the same thing for two weeks: that bite is steady, not special. Small fish, a keeper here and there, nothing to write home about. If that's your speed, fine, but I've been putting my hours in somewhere else — the rock pile on the east side of Jones Inlet, after the sun goes down, working the current seams where the real bass have been holding.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear: the ocean's been ugly. Close-period chop, three-plus feet of slop rolling in off the bar, not the kind of water that makes for good beach fishing off Jones Beach right now. So the fish that would normally be working the wash have pulled inside — into the inlet channel, along the rocks, up into the deeper current cuts where the water stays clean and the bait gets funneled through on the tide. That's exactly where I've been finding bass. Not giant numbers, but quality — 28 to 34 inches, a few pushing better than that, holding tight to the jetty rocks on the last two hours of the outgoing and right through the bottom of the tide into the first push of the flood.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the deep, current-driven bite would hold until either a cooling trend or the new moon tide stirred things up. Well, the new moon's two days out now, and I'm already feeling the difference in the swing. Tuesday night's drift through the inlet channel moved noticeably harder than it did a week ago, and the bass responded — three fish in the slot in about ninety minutes on a bucktail-and-eel combo, 3/4-ounce bucktail with a 6-inch white worm trailer, worked slow along the base of the rocks where the current breaks. If you're fishing bait, fresh bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, tossed into the seam where the jetty meets the main channel, has been getting hit consistently right around the tide change — that dead-slack window when everything settles and the fish move up to feed before the current builds back the other way.

Bluefish are the other piece I've had my eye on. We called this too — said the bluefish wave building down in Jersey and around Sandy Hook could push north and reinforce the bite here, and I think that's starting to happen. I had a mixed bag Wednesday morning working bunker schools just inside the inlet mouth — mostly bass, but two bluefish in the 4 to 6-pound class mixed in, hit on a Hopkins jig worked fast through the school. Nothing like a blitz yet, but the bait's there and the blues are starting to show up behind it. If that northward push keeps building the way it did in Jersey, don't be surprised if the next week or two turns into real bluefish weather at the inlet — keep a wire leader in the bag just in case.

Weakfish are still the sleeper story in Hempstead Bay this summer, and I don't think enough guys are paying attention to it. South Oyster Bay, especially the deeper holes off Freeport and up toward the Wantagh Bridge, has been holding weakfish that'll actually pull drag — nothing gigantic, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but that's a real comeback for a fish that's been an afterthought around here for a decade. Grass shrimp under a float, fished slow along the channel edges at dusk, or a small bucktail tipped with squid worked right along bottom near the bridge pilings on the last of the incoming — that's been the ticket. Fish it quiet, fish it slow, and don't horse them — weakfish have paper mouths and you'll lose half of what you hook if you're not patient.

Looking ahead, the new moon on the 12th is going to swing the tides hard, and that's usually when this inlet turns on. Bigger current means more bait getting pushed through the cut, which means the bass and blues stack up tighter on the structure instead of spreading out across the flats. If I had to pick one window for the next week, I'd take the two nights around the new moon, fishing the rocks from an hour before the tide turns through the first hour of the flood. The fluke in Sloop Channel will still be there if you want an easy afternoon, but if you want to feel a real fish bend a rod, the jetty's earning its name again. Bring a headlamp, bring patience, and don't be the guy still parked in the fluke drift when the real bite's happening twenty minutes away in the dark.
